record.paper_title: Open Problems in Hydrodynamical Approach to Relativistic Heavy Ion Collisions
record.original_question: How can one determine whether the collective flow observed in relativistic heavy-ion collision data is genuinely hydrodynamic behavior based on local thermodynamical equilibrium, rather than a flow pattern produced by non-equilibrium dynamics that still obey local energy-momentum conservation or other force mechanisms?

evidence.quote: This is basically because the starting assumption of the validity of local thermodynamical equilibrium in hydrodynamics is not at all trivial to be justified for microscopic systems.
When we use the equation of state to describe the pressure as function of density, the hydrodynamical equations are meaningful only if the approximation of local thermal equilibrium is valid.
That is, a flow phenomena does not necessarily indicates the validity of the local thermodynamical equilibrium.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In an ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collision, the produced matter exhibits collective flow patterns (e.g., radial flow, elliptic flow, and higher azimuthal anisotropy coefficients v_n) in the measured single-particle momentum distributions. A standard interpretation models the produced system as a relativistic fluid governed by the conservation laws ∂_μ T^{μν} = 0 with an equation of state p = p(ε) that is only meaningful under the assumption of local thermodynamical equilibrium (i.e., the existence at each spacetime point of a local 4-velocity u^μ and thermodynamic variables such that the energy–momentum tensor takes the ideal-fluid form T^{μν} = (ε+p)u^μ u^ν − p g^{μν}, possibly with small dissipative corrections). However, similar collective flow patterns can in principle be generated by non-equilibrium microscopic dynamics that nevertheless respect local energy–momentum conservation (e.g., few-rescattering transport, free-streaming with later kinetic freeze-out, color-field-driven dynamics, or other force mechanisms) without ever achieving local thermal equilibrium.

Problem. Formulate criteria — based on experimentally accessible observables in relativistic heavy-ion collision data — that can decisively determine whether the observed collective flow is genuinely hydrodynamic in origin, i.e., arises from an evolution in which the assumption of local thermodynamical equilibrium is valid (so that the use of an equation of state p(ε) in the hydrodynamic equations is justified), as opposed to being a flow pattern produced by non-equilibrium dynamics consistent with local energy–momentum conservation or other (non-thermal) force mechanisms. Provide an unambiguous procedure (a set of observables and/or correlations together with predicted signatures) that distinguishes these two scenarios.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent work (2024–2025) continues to address this question by comparing kinetic-theory to viscous-hydrodynamic simulations and by proposing observables that quantify the degree of hydrodynamic behavior, especially in small systems where local equilibrium is questionable. These works treat the issue as still under active investigation rather than settled, indicating the problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: Collective dynamics in heavy and light-ion collisions — I) Kinetic Theory vs. Hydrodynamics
status_evidence.snippet: Quantify to what extent a macroscopic hydrodynamic description can accurately describe the development of collective flow, and to what extent collective flow in small systems is sensitive to the non-equilibrium evolution beyond hydrodynamics.
status_evidence.claim: Active 2024 study still investigating whether collective flow is genuinely hydrodynamic or has significant non-equilibrium origin.

status_evidence.title: Quantifying the degree of hydrodynamic behaviour in heavy-ion collisions
status_evidence.snippet: Proposes experimentally accessible observable to distinguish whether collective behaviour builds up through hydrodynamic expansion of a strongly interacting QGP or through few rescatterings in a non-equilibrated dilute medium.
status_evidence.claim: As of 2025 researchers are still proposing new observables to discriminate hydrodynamic from non-equilibrium origins of collective flow, indicating the question is open.
